name: ML Privacy & Model Security
description: Privacy attacks against ML (membership inference, model/data extraction, inversion) and federated-learning security.

ccs.narrative:
ML privacy research at CCS has dissected the information leakage surface of machine learning systems from multiple angles. The 2018 class introduced three foundational attack categories: Property Inference Attacks on Fully Connected Neural Networks using Permutation Invariant Representations (CCS 2018) extracted global training-set statistics, Machine Learning with Membership Privacy using Adversarial Regularization (CCS 2018) studied membership inference defenses, and Secure Outsourced Matrix Computation and Application to Neural Networks (CCS 2018) explored privacy-preserving inference via FHE.

The 2019-2020 period extended attacks to new model classes and sharpened defenses. MemGuard: Defending against Black-Box Membership Inference Attacks via Adversarial Examples (CCS 2019) added noise to confidence scores to protect membership status, while GAN-Leaks: A Taxonomy of Membership Inference Attacks against Generative Models (CCS 2020) and Information Leakage in Embedding Models (CCS 2020) broadened the threat beyond classifiers to generative and embedding models.

From 2022, federated learning became a central battleground. Enhanced Membership Inference Attacks against Machine Learning Models (CCS 2022) formalized attack evaluation as hypothesis testing, and Eluding Secure Aggregation in Federated Learning via Model Inconsistency (CCS 2022) showed that a malicious server can break secure aggregation. Truth Serum: Poisoning Machine Learning Models to Reveal Their Secrets (CCS 2022) revealed that poisoning amplifies privacy leakage, linking adversarial ML and ML privacy.

milestones.title: Property Inference Attacks on Fully Connected Neural Networks using Permutation Invariant Representations
milestones.note: Showed neural networks leak global dataset properties, establishing property inference as a distinct attack class.

milestones.title: Machine Learning with Membership Privacy using Adversarial Regularization
milestones.note: Proposed adversarial regularization as a training-time defense making models resistant to membership inference.

milestones.title: MemGuard: Defending against Black-Box Membership Inference Attacks via Adversarial Examples
milestones.note: Added carefully crafted noise to prediction confidence scores to deny membership inference attackers useful signals.

milestones.title: GAN-Leaks: A Taxonomy of Membership Inference Attacks against Generative Models
milestones.note: Systematized membership inference against GANs, expanding the threat beyond discriminative classifiers.

milestones.title: Information Leakage in Embedding Models
milestones.note: Demonstrated that text embedding models leak input attributes and can be inverted to recover sensitive data.

milestones.title: Enhanced Membership Inference Attacks against Machine Learning Models
milestones.note: Framed membership inference as hypothesis testing, producing stronger attacks that better audit training-data leakage.

milestones.title: Eluding Secure Aggregation in Federated Learning via Model Inconsistency
milestones.note: Broke federated learning's secure aggregation guarantee by exploiting model inconsistency on a malicious server.

milestones.title: Truth Serum: Poisoning Machine Learning Models to Reveal Their Secrets
milestones.note: Showed that data poisoning amplifies membership and attribute leakage, connecting adversarial and privacy ML threats.

ndss.narrative:
ML privacy and model security at NDSS has been one of the fastest-moving areas in the dataset. The inaugural Trojaning Attack on Neural Networks (NDSS 2018) showed that backdoors can be surgically inserted into trained models, achieving over 1,300 citations and effectively founding a sub-field. Within two years the community had generalized this threat: ML-Leaks (NDSS 2019) demonstrated model-agnostic membership inference, and CloudLeak (NDSS 2020) showed that commercial MLaaS APIs leak enough information to reconstruct large models.

The 2021–2022 period addressed federated learning's particular vulnerabilities. Manipulating the Byzantine (NDSS 2021) optimized model poisoning attacks in federated settings, while DeepSight (NDSS 2022) proposed deep-structure inspection to detect backdoored updates without access to raw data—both papers achieving high citation counts that reflect the field's rapid growth.

From 2023 onward the community has moved toward protecting and auditing deployed models. REDsec (NDSS 2023) made encrypted inference on discretized neural networks practical; Automatic Adversarial Adaption for Stealthy Poisoning Attacks in Federated Learning (NDSS 2024) showed that poisoning attacks can be adapted to evade modern defenses; and I Know What You Asked (NDSS 2025) exposed prompt leakage via KV-cache sharing in multi-tenant LLM deployments, connecting the ML-privacy agenda to the new era of large language models.

milestones.title: Trojaning Attack on Neural Networks
milestones.note: Trojans neural networks by crafting triggers and retraining, causing targeted misbehavior on inputs with the trigger.

milestones.title: ML-Leaks: Model and Data Independent Membership Inference Attacks and Defenses on Machine Learning Models
milestones.note: Shows membership inference attacks work without model or data knowledge and proposes defenses against them.

milestones.title: CloudLeak: Large-Scale Deep Learning Models Stealing Through Adversarial Examples
milestones.note: Steals cloud-hosted deep learning models efficiently using adversarial examples to query and reconstruct them.

milestones.title: Manipulating the Byzantine: Optimizing Model Poisoning Attacks and Defenses for Federated Learning
milestones.note: Optimizes model-poisoning attacks against federated learning and evaluates corresponding byzantine-robust defenses.

milestones.title: DeepSight: Mitigating Backdoor Attacks in Federated Learning Through Deep Model Inspection
milestones.note: Mitigates backdoor poisoning in federated learning through deep inspection of submitted model updates.

milestones.title: REDsec: Running Encrypted Discretized Neural Networks in Seconds
milestones.note: REDsec runs discretized neural networks under fully homomorphic encryption efficiently, enabling privacy-preserving inference in seconds.

milestones.title: Automatic Adversarial Adaption for Stealthy Poisoning Attacks in Federated Learning
milestones.note: Develops stealthy adaptive poisoning attacks that evade defenses in federated learning by automatically adjusting to detection mechanisms.

milestones.title: I Know What You Asked: Prompt Leakage via KV-Cache Sharing in Multi-Tenant LLM Serving
milestones.note: Shows shared KV-cache in multi-tenant LLM serving leaks other users' prompts.

sp.narrative:
ML privacy research at IEEE S&P examines how training and inference leak private data. The landmark 2019 papers set the agenda for the entire field. Comprehensive Privacy Analysis of Deep Learning: Passive and Active White-box Inference Attacks against Centralized and Federated Learning (S&P 2019) gave the first systematic membership-inference taxonomy across centralized and federated settings. Exploiting Unintended Feature Leakage in Collaborative Learning (S&P 2019) showed federated-learning gradients expose raw training data via reconstruction. Stealing Hyperparameters in Machine Learning (S&P 2018) had already established that model-theft extends beyond weights.

Differentially-private training emerged as the canonical defense target. Differentially Private Model Publishing for Deep Learning (S&P 2019) and Towards Practical Differentially Private Convex Optimization (S&P 2019) worked to close the accuracy gap between DP and non-private models. CrypTFlow: Secure TensorFlow Inference (S&P 2020) took a different route, using MPC to protect model inputs at inference time. Privacy Risks of General-Purpose Language Models (S&P 2020) extended membership inference to large language models.

Machine Unlearning (S&P 2021) opened a new front: the right to remove a specific individual's data from an already-trained model, a problem that grew more pressing with GDPR enforcement. Membership Inference Attacks From First Principles (S&P 2022) provided the cleanest theoretical characterization of when membership inference is possible, and Adversary Instantiation: Lower Bounds for Differentially Private Machine Learning (S&P 2021) established the limits of DP protection.

By 2023-2024, Analyzing Leakage of Personally Identifiable Information in Language Models (S&P 2023) showed that foundation models memorize and reproduce PII at alarming rates. The topic increasingly overlaps with LLM security and supply-chain poisoning as the models under scrutiny grow in scale and deployment breadth.

uss.narrative:
The earliest papers in this list, all from USENIX Security 2018, mark the moment when ML privacy and model security crystallized into a distinct research agenda. The work split along two lines that still organize the field. One line was defensive and protective: "AttriGuard: A Practical Defense Against Attribute Inference Attacks via Adversarial Machine Learning" (USENIX 2018) used adversarial perturbations to stop attackers from inferring users' hidden attributes, while "Turning Your Weakness Into a Strength: Watermarking Deep Neural Networks by Backdooring" (USENIX 2018) repurposed backdoors as a tool for claiming model ownership. The other line was offensive, exposing how much models leak: "With Great Training Comes Great Vulnerability: Practical Attacks against Transfer Learning" (USENIX 2018) showed that the now-common practice of fine-tuning shared backbones opens a clear attack surface, and "GAZELLE: A Low Latency Framework for Secure Neural Network Inference" (USENIX 2018) began the parallel effort to run inference without exposing data at all.

Around 2019-2020 the field grew more rigorous and more physical. "Evaluating Differentially Private Machine Learning in Practice" (USENIX 2019) pushed past theory to ask what a privacy budget really buys, becoming a reference point for honest accounting of DP defenses. At the same time, attackers moved off the math and onto the hardware: "CSI NN: Reverse Engineering of Neural Network Architectures Through Electromagnetic Side Channel" (USENIX 2019) and "Stealthy Tracking of Autonomous Vehicles with Cache Side Channels" (USENIX 2020) showed that side channels can steal architectures and track real systems. "Fawkes: Protecting Privacy against Unauthorized Deep Learning Models" (USENIX 2020) turned the protective instinct toward ordinary users, cloaking photos against facial recognition scrapers like Clearview.ai.

By 2022-2023 attention shifted decisively toward distributed training and generative models, and the volume of work exploded. Federated and split learning became a battleground: "FLAME: Taming Backdoors in Federated Learning" (USENIX 2022) defended the global model, while attacks like "VILLAIN: Backdoor Attacks Against Vertical Split Learning" (USENIX 2023) and "PCAT: Functionality and Data Stealing from Split Learning by Pseudo-Client Attack" (USENIX 2023) showed that splitting a model does not by itself protect the data inside it. Generative models brought their own crisis of memorization: "Extracting Training Data from Diffusion Models" (USENIX 2023), one of the most-cited papers here, demonstrated that image generators regurgitate their training data verbatim, and "CodexLeaks: Privacy Leaks from Code Generation Language Models in GitHub Copilot" (USENIX 2023) showed the same problem for code models in production.

Most recently the field has been responding to the dominance of large generative and foundation models on both the attack and defense sides. Defenses now aim to make generation itself private, as in "dp-promise: Differentially Private Diffusion Probabilistic Models for Image Synthesis" (USENIX 2024), and to harden deployed APIs against theft, as in "ModelGuard: Information-Theoretic Defense Against Model Extraction Attacks" (USENIX 2024). Cryptographic verifiability has matured from the inference frameworks of GAZELLE into scalable proofs, with "Scalable Zero-knowledge Proofs for Non-linear Functions in Machine Learning" (USENIX 2024). And the classic membership-inference question that animated the early work has been carried into the LLM era by "Towards Label-Only Membership Inference Attack against Pre-trained Large Language Models" (USENIX 2025), showing that even with only label access, one can probe what a large model has seen. The throughline across all these venues is a steady escalation: each new training paradigm and model class reopens the same privacy questions on harder terrain.

top4.narrative:
The earliest work in this list splits along two lines that would define the field. On the attack side, "Trojaning Attack on Neural Networks" (NDSS 2018) showed that shared, publicly distributed models could be quietly subverted, while a cluster of 2018 papers turned the lens on what models leak: "Property Inference Attacks on Fully Connected Neural Networks" (CCS 2018) and "Stealing Hyperparameters in Machine Learning" (S&P 2018) demonstrated that even abstract properties and training settings could be recovered from a model. In parallel, defenders began responding both with empirical patches like "Machine Learning with Membership Privacy using Adversarial Regularization" (CCS 2018) and "AttriGuard" (USENIX 2018), and with cryptographic privacy via secure inference systems such as "GAZELLE" (USENIX 2018) and "Secure Outsourced Matrix Computation" (CCS 2018).

The 2019 wave sharpened membership and inference attacks into a science and pushed them into the collaborative setting. "Comprehensive Privacy Analysis of Deep Learning" (S&P 2019) and "Exploiting Unintended Feature Leakage in Collaborative Learning" (S&P 2019) showed that federated and centralized training both leak, including through white-box and active adversaries — connecting privacy leakage directly to the distributed-training agenda that would later dominate. This period also matured the defense toolkit: differential privacy moved from theory to scrutiny with "Evaluating Differentially Private Machine Learning in Practice" (USENIX 2019) and "Differentially Private Model Publishing for Deep Learning" (S&P 2019), trojan detection emerged with "ABS" (CCS 2019), and "Neural Network Inversion in Adversarial Setting" (CCS 2019) extended leakage to reconstructing inputs. A recurring theme — that defenses can backfire — appeared in "Privacy Risks of Securing Machine Learning Models against Adversarial Examples" (CCS 2019).

By 2020-2021 the targets broadened from classifiers to generative and language models, and the field grew more self-critical. "GAN-Leaks" (CCS 2020), "Information Leakage in Embedding Models" (CCS 2020), and "Privacy Risks of General-Purpose Language Models" (S&P 2020) extended membership and reconstruction attacks to GANs, embeddings, and large LMs, while "Fawkes" (USENIX 2020) turned privacy attacks into a user-facing protection against facial recognition. "Machine Unlearning" (S&P 2021) opened the right-to-be-forgotten subfield, immediately complicated by "When Machine Unlearning Jeopardizes Privacy" (CCS 2021). Federated learning security crystallized around poisoning attacks and defenses with "Manipulating the Byzantine" (NDSS 2021), and "Adversary Instantiation" (S&P 2021) reframed DP guarantees as concrete lower bounds.

The current frontier, reflected in 2022-2023, is rigor and scale. "Membership Inference Attacks From First Principles" (S&P 2022) and "Enhanced Membership Inference Attacks" (CCS 2022) re-grounded the canonical attack in proper statistical evaluation, while federated defenses were stress-tested by "Back to the Drawing Board" (S&P 2022) against the more practical mitigations "FLAME" (USENIX 2022) and "DeepSight" (NDSS 2022). Most strikingly, "Extracting Training Data from Diffusion Models" (USENIX 2023) and "Analyzing Leakage of Personally Identifiable Information in Language Models" (S&P 2023) showed that today's largest generative models memorize and regurgitate verbatim training data — moving the field from "can we infer membership?" to "we can extract the data itself," now the dominant concern for foundation models.
